transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-09-14
Time: 16:30 PT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Daniel (Silverbay Head of Compliance), Maya (Platform), Ravi (CISO)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Silverbay is evaluating hosting options for a lending decisioning assistant. Primary concerns: GDPR personal data flow, financial controls, log retention limits, keystore residency and legal-hold workflows. Team wants clear boundaries for what we store, how logs are redacted, and options for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment.

[00:00] Aisha: okay hey everybody thanks for joining, appreciate it. quick intros before we dive in.
[00:08] Daniel: hi yes daniel here, head of compliance at Silverbay. we run underwriting and risk models, we want to understand how your platform handles sensitive borrower PII and, uh, audit trails.
[00:17] Maya: maya here, i'll be the platform owner, curious about network controls, VPC options, and -- sorry -- key management.
[00:22] Ravi: ravi, ciso. main thing for me is legal hold, egress controls, and making sure nothing crosses jurisdictions without explicit routing rules.
[00:29] Marcus: thanks all, i'm marcus, solutions engineer with redwood, i'll cover runtime and logging. quick agenda: residency and routing, logging and redaction, keystore/KMS, and next steps.

[02:11] Aisha: to start, can you walk through your high-level constraints and timeline? are you looking for a pilot or production roll?
[02:20] Daniel: pilot first. we want a 6–8 week POC, ideally in us-east-1, but some customers are in the EU so we need to ensure eu personal data stays in eu region when required. we are heavily regulated — SOC2 plus financial regulations here, and certain datasets are HIPAA-adjacent because of medical debt data.
[02:45] Marcus: understood. rough topology options we see: Redwood Hosted (fastest), Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pool single-tenant), Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem). each has different controls: Hosted can offer region pinning but logs may transit central control plane depending on options; Dedicated gives stronger isolation and control-plane telemetry can be minimized; Private gives max control (control plane customer-managed).

[04:12] Maya: what's the default log retention and can we opt to prevent transcript storage of PII? we do not want raw prompts persisted for more than 7 days in any case.
[04:23] Marcus: default retention for hosted customers is 30 days for request/response logs for debugging, but you can configure data-minimization policies and redaction. for dedicated we can set retention to 7 days or less and disable transcript persistence entirely if you provide a retention SLA. note: some runtime telemetry (metrics) is retained for service health longer but is aggregated.

[05:45] Ravi: i want to hear more about live redaction. can redwood do PII masking before data hits persistent logs? e.g. redact account numbers, ssn-like tokens, names?
[05:58] Marcus: yes we have a couple of approaches — client-side pre-processing (recommended), and server-side live redaction. server-side redaction uses configurable regex and ML-based detectors (we call it "sieve" internally but uh apologies the auto-transcript sometimes shows wrong product names) that can scrub values before they hit long-term storage. caveat: server-side redaction still touches the data in memory during inference unless you're using a private deployment with customer-managed keystore and in-memory protections.
[06:38] Daniel: so for GDPR, how do we prove we aren't transferring data to the US when the model is in eu-west-1 but the control plane is centralized?
[06:48] Marcus: good question. for hosted we offer regional routing where inference and logs remain in-region; however control plane metadata (billing, route decisions) may still traverse us control plane under certain configurations. Dedicated customers can opt for regional control plane replicas and Private provides customer-managed control plane so nothing leaves their network. we also offer contractual data residency clauses and SCCs for EU customers.

[08:12] Maya: can you do keystore residency? we need keys to be held in our KMS (aws-kms or cloud-hsm) and never exported.
[08:21] Marcus: yes, for Private deployment we integrate with customer KMS/HSM using local key wrapping. for Dedicated we can support BYOK (bring-your-own-key) with HSM-backed providers and key escrow options. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer KMS but the control plane handles key rotation unless you choose a private keystore option.

[09:34] Ravi: on legal hold — if regulators ask for a tranche of transactions from 18 months ago, can we provide redacted transcripts only? and how do you handle audit logs for that request?
[09:46] Marcus: we support audit exports with configurable retention tiers. you can mark transcripts as redacted at export time or keep immutable audit copies in a restricted archive. for legal hold we can snapshot archives into a long-term store (S3) with customer-specified encryption and access policies; those snapshots can be programmatically restricted to a small vault and only exposed via an auditable flow.

[11:05] Daniel: what's the risk surface for model cache (KV cache)? we worry about leakage if earlier prompts persist in shared cache.
[11:16] Marcus: Redwood runtime uses isolated KV cache per tenant and per model session for Dedicated/Private; for Hosted low-tier multitenant we rely on strict namespace isolation but we can disable persistent KV caching if you want to remove any chance of cross-tenant leakage. also you can pin model versions to avoid implicit cache reuse across rollouts.

[13:00] Maya: what about token-level billing visibility? our finance team wants to map tokens to business units without exposing PII in billing metadata.
[13:09] Marcus: we emit token counts and cost breakdowns at route and token-level metadata — but you can scrub request content from telemetry. billing metadata is separate and can be anonymized. we also provide per-route dashboards in Redwood Console so you can map costs to BU without storing prompt text.

[15:44] Aisha: any specific compliance docs we should send right now?
[15:49] Daniel: if we could get SOC2 and ISO evidence plus a short note on how you handle eu control-plane traffic that would be ideal. also we want a doc describing redaction workflow and options for live masking.

[17:02] Marcus: we'll attach SOC2+ISO summary and a one-page keystore/residency note; i'll also draft a short runbook on live-redaction flows (client-side vs server-side) with tradeoffs.

[18:20] Ravi: one more question — are background model telemetry or embeddings retained and could they be reconstructed to expose data?
[18:31] Marcus: embeddings can be configured to not be persisted. default hosted embeddings retention is 30 days for search caching, but we can configure ephemeral embeddings that never hit disk. regarding reconstruction: we have detection for high-entropy vectors and we treat embeddings as sensitive by default when marked by customers; other protections include quantization and hashing and optional client-side vectorization.

[20:00] Maya: what's the path for us to test hosted vs dedicated? we have a small traffic slice we want to run in us-east and eu-west simultaneously for behavior and latency comparison.
[20:12] Marcus: typical POC is: 1) we provision a dedicated sandbox project in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 with pinned models; 2) you provide a representative prompt set and traffic; 3) we run benchmark tests for 2–3 weeks and produce latency and cost report. Hosted is fastest to start but you'll want a dedicated run for production-like isolation.

[22:15] Daniel: cost tradeoffs — if we reduce retention and disable transcripts, how much does that reduce hosted costs?
[22:26] Marcus: retention and logging add to storage and egress costs; rough rule-of-thumb: reducing retention from 30d to 7d drops storage-related fees by 60–70% for logs, and disabling transcript storage can reduce debugging overhead and long-term archival costs. batching/quantization recommendations from Redwood Optimize can further reduce per-token cost. we'll give a customized estimate in the POC pricing sheet.

[24:58] Aisha: side note — are there any certifications for financial controls beyond SOC2 that you can share?
[25:05] Marcus: we have SOC2 type II and ISO 27001. for finance-specific controls we provide audit mapping docs on request; some customers ask us to fill in SSAE/ISAE mappings and we can provide that for the procurement path.

[26:40] Maya: network-wise, can we run the inference endpoints inside our VPC with private link so no public egress?
[26:49] Marcus: yes — Private supports on-prem or VPC-deployed inference where endpoints sit inside your VPC. Dedicated supports private connectivity (VPC peering or PrivateLink) and you can restrict egress entirely. Hosted supports PrivateLink options for enterprise plans but some control-plane interactions may still use Redwood's management plane unless you choose the Private offering.

[29:02] Ravi: about SSO and RBAC — can we centralize auth via SAML/SCIM and restrict access to logs by role?
[29:12] Marcus: yes SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning supported across all tiers; RBAC is customizable so you can restrict access to redaction controls, legal exports, and keystore operations to specific roles. we also support audit trails for who exported what and when.

[31:30] Daniel: curious about multijurisdictional fallback routing: if eu cluster is saturated can traffic fail over to us region but still meet gdpr constraints?
[31:44] Marcus: fallback routing is policy-driven. you can configure strict residency guardrails that block failover outside region (preferred for GDPR strict mode), or you can allow failover to a specific compatible region with masking and additional consent clauses. fallback behavior is logged and you can trigger alerts for any cross-border failover. contractual controls + technical enforcement both available.

[34:10] Maya: we need to model a scenario: a legal hold requiring preservation of a set of user interactions across EU and US customers — what's the simplest recommended approach?
[34:24] Marcus: simplest is snapshotting the relevant logs into your long-term archive in-region with customer-managed encryption keys, mark them immutable, and apply limited-access policies. if EU data is involved, ensure snapshots are stored in an EU bucket; for Hosted we can orchestrate that with an EU-only export flow. Private gives you end-to-end control.

[36:55] Ravi: does redwood provide any support for pseudonymization patterns we might adopt? we want the ability to replace direct identifiers with reversible tokens under our KMS so we can rehydrate only under legal process.
[37:07] Marcus: yes that's a common pattern. recommended flow: client-side pseudonymization with reversible tokenization under your KMS; inference works on tokenized values so redwood never sees raw identifiers. rehydration requires decryption under your control. we can also support a server-side token service in Private deployments if you need centralized tokenization.

[39:42] Daniel: any gotchas around backups and snapshots that might leak PII?
[39:51] Marcus: standard: double-check snapshot destinations, ensure encryption keys are the customer-managed ones, and ensure that logs marked for short retention are excluded from backups. we include an export manifest that shows exactly what was archived.

[42:00] Maya: from an ops perspective, can we get a runbook that describes who to call for an incident and the expected response SLAs for data-exposure events?
[42:12] Marcus: yes we'll provide an incident runbook and SLA matrix; Dedicated and Private have quicker on-call SLAs and a support escalation path. Hosted has standard priority response times documented in the SLA.

[44:30] Aisha: ok let's recap next steps quickly.
[44:35] Daniel: we'll run a pilot but only after we review the SOC2 packet and the keystore/residency note. we need answers on: 1) whether embedded vectors can be ephemeral, 2) legal-hold snapshot flow, 3) live redaction tradeoffs.
[44:50] Aisha: action recap — redwood to send SOC2/ISO and keystore/residency note (aisha), marcus to produce live-redaction runbook and ephemeral embeddings note, maya to share sample prompt set and PII categories.

[46:12] Ravi: one final small thing — encryption in transit and at rest specifics? we require TLS1.3 for all endpoints and customer-keyed AES-256 for at-rest.
[46:25] Marcus: we support TLS 1.2 and 1.3; enterprise plans can enforce TLS1.3 only. at-rest encryption supports AES-256 with customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations.

[48:00] Maya: ok timeline — can you get the docs over by next week?
[48:07] Aisha: yes we will target sept 18 for docs, bench scheduling the following week, and a kickoff for the POC on sept 23 if that works for you.

[50:18] Daniel: sounds good. also please include an explicit note about control-plane telemetry — we need to know which attributes might cross borders for hosted offering.
[50:28] Marcus: noted, i'll add a control-plane attribute matrix to the residency note.

[51:10] Aisha: thanks everyone, any other final questions?
[51:17] Maya: none from me.
[51:19] Ravi: no.
[51:20] Daniel: nothing else. thanks all.

[53:45] Aisha: great thanks we'll follow up with the packet and next steps. have a good afternoon.

End of transcript.
